n: Gross Anatomy Spotters for Clinical Exams

faq.a: The spleen is softer, has a smooth capsule, and its hilum faces medially; the kidney is firmer, has a cortical‑medullary distinction, and a renal sinus.
faq.q: How can I differentiate the spleen from the left kidney on a cadaveric specimen?

faq.a: Look for a pear‑shaped anechoic structure between the liver’s right lobe and the visceral surface of the quadrate lobe, under the rib cage.
faq.q: What landmark helps locate the gallbladder on a bedside ultrasound?

faq.a: It is a low‑contrast soft‑tissue structure; only enlarged or thrombosed veins may produce indirect signs such as collateral vessels.
faq.q: Why is the portal vein not visible on a plain X‑ray?

exam: Identify the organ shown and explain why a patient with malaria might have it enlarged — note size, location and malaria‑related congestion.
You see a firm, bean‑shaped mass in the right flank on a CT slice; what is it and what emergency complication must you rule out? — Kidney; rule out obstructive uropathy or renal infarction.

During a bedside exam a patient has dullness to percussion in the left flank that shifts when they turn — what does this indicate and what is the next bedside step? — Ascites; perform paracentesis if safe.

A photograph shows a triangular area of peritoneum between the liver and stomach; name it and its clinical significance in perforated ulcer. — Lesser sac; fluid may collect here, prompting focused ultrasound.

You are asked to point out the hepatic portal triad on a liver cross‑section; list its three components and why injury to it causes jaundice. — Hepatic artery, portal vein, bile duct; obstruction of bile flow leads to cholestatic jaundice.

A patient presents with left upper quadrant pain after a fall; the spotter shows a ruptured spleen — what immediate management is required in a low‑resource setting? — Stabilise haemodynamics, arrange urgent splenectomy or packing if blood products scarce.
Explain why the right kidney is often higher than the left on a supine radiograph. — The liver pushes the right kidney superiorly; important when assessing for renal displacement.

You see a bulging, pulsatile mass in the abdomen on inspection; which vessel is most likely involved and what bedside test confirms it? — Abdominal aortic aneurysm; check for a palpable thrill and use bedside Doppler if available.
ai.title: Gross Anatomy Spotters for Clinical Exams
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: A concise guide to identifying key anatomical structures on gross specimens and imaging, linking location to clinical signs and common low‑resource challenges.

b: Focus on surface landmarks, organ shape, relationships and typical pathologies seen in East African hospitals.
sections.p: Spotters test the ability to recognise organs, vessels and spaces on cadaveric specimens, photographs or bedside imaging, then relate them to presenting symptoms.

b: Liver – right upper quadrant, smooth convex surface, falciform ligament on anterior surface.
Spleen – left upper quadrant, tucked under 9th‑11th ribs, hilum faces medially.
Kidney – retroperitoneal, flank region, bean‑shaped, renal hilum faces medially.
sections.p: Describe the size, shape, borders and typical position of each structure in the supine and upright patient.

b: Stomach lies anterior to pancreas; duodenum wraps around pancreatic head.
Ascending colon is retroperitoneal, lateral to the right kidney.
sections.p: Know what lies anterior, posterior, superior and inferior to each organ to avoid misidentification.

b: Hepatic artery proper and portal vein supply the liver; hepatic veins drain into IVC.
Renal artery enters at the hilum; renal vein exits at the same level.
sections.p: Identify the main arterial and venous sources that are visible on gross specimens or Doppler ultrasound.

b: Greater splanchnic nerves (T5‑9) convey visceral pain from the liver and gallbladder.
Phrenic nerve (C3‑5) supplies diaphragmatic pleura; irritation causes shoulder tip pain.
sections.p: Highlight autonomic and somatic innervation relevant to pain patterns and reflex testing.

b: Liver detoxifies blood, produces clotting factors; failure leads to coagulopathy.
Kidney filters plasma, regulates electrolytes; obstruction causes flank pain and oliguria.
sections.p: Briefly link structure to physiological role that may explain clinical findings.

b: Palpable enlarged liver in malaria‑related hepatic congestion.
Splenomegaly from malaria, schistosomiasis or sickle‑cell disease.
Renal cortical necrosis after severe sepsis or hemolytic crisis.
sections.p: Connect each spotter to common presentations in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Confirms organ size and internal echotexture when visual inspection is ambiguous; if unavailable, rely on percussion and shifting dullness.
Distinguishes hepatic from hemolytic jaundice; if lab not available, assess scleral colour and urine darkening.

b: Always state organ, side, and one clinical implication.
Mention a common local disease that would enlarge or alter the organ.
sections.p: Key tricks examiners use to test spotters and how to answer efficiently.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden abdominal distension with absent bowel sounds – possible perforated viscus.
Rapidly enlarging tender liver – acute hepatic failure.
